summary.title: Visualization of π-hole in molecules by means of Kelvin probe force microscopy
summary.authors: B Mallada; M Ondráček; M Lamanec; A Gallardo; A Jiménez-Martín; B De La Torre; P Hobza; P Jelínek
summary.executive_summary: This study provides the first direct experimental visualization of the π-hole, a submolecular electron-deficient cavity, in 9,10-Dichlorooctafluoroanthracene (FCl-An) using Kelvin Probe Force Microscopy (KPFM). While the existence of π-holes was previously predicted by quantum calculations and inferred indirectly from intermolecular interaction data, this work confirms their presence by mapping the local contact potential difference (LCPD) with atomic resolution. The researchers compared FCl-An with unsubstituted anthracene (An) on an Au(111) surface. Results show that FCl-An exhibits a characteristic 'bow-tie' pattern in LCPD maps, corresponding to the positive electrostatic potential of the π-hole, whereas An does not. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the π-hole significantly alters the molecule's interaction with the metallic substrate. Specifically, the π-hole increases the ionization potential of FCl-An, which suppresses charge induction at the molecule/metal interface. This leads to weaker induced electrostatic interactions and a measurable increase in the adsorption height of FCl-An compared to An. The findings validate theoretical predictions regarding the role of submolecular charge distribution in non-covalent interactions and adsorption phenomena, highlighting KPFM as a powerful tool for real-space observation of molecular electrostatics.

The π-hole increases the adsorption height of the molecule on a metallic substrate.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study provides the first direct experimental visualization of the π-hole, a submolecular electron-deficient cavity, in 9,10-Dichlorooctafluoroanthracene (FCl-An) using Kelvin Probe Force Microscopy (KPFM). While the existence of π-holes was previously predicted by quantum calculations and inferred indirectly from intermolecular interaction data, this work confirms their presence by mapping the local contact potential difference (LCPD) with atomic resolution. The researchers compared FCl-An with unsubstituted anthracene (An) on an Au(111) surface. Results show that FCl-An exhibits a characteristic 'bow-tie' pattern in LCPD maps, corresponding to the positive electrostatic potential of the π-hole, whereas An does not. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the π-hole significantly alters the molecule's interaction with the metallic substrate. Specifically, the π-hole increases the ionization potential of FCl-An, which suppresses charge induction at the molecule/metal interface. This leads to weaker induced electrostatic interactions and a measurable increase in the adsorption height of FCl-An compared to An. The findings validate theoretical predictions regarding the role of submolecular charge distribution in non-covalent interactions and adsorption phenomena, highlighting KPFM as a powerful tool for real-space observation of molecular electrostatics.

Research Context
Non-covalent interactions are crucial in many chemical and biological processes. The nature of the electrostatic interaction is intimately linked to the internal charge distribution. In polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, substituents can reverse the electron population of the π-bond system. The presence of a π-electron-deficient cavity in the central part of the molecule is called a π-hole. The concept of π-hole has been developed exclusively on a theoretical basis using quantum calculations. A direct experimental observation that would clearly prove the existence of the π-hole has been lacking. Scanning probe microscopy (SPM) emerges as the most appropriate tool for the direct visualization of π-holes.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to resolve the π-hole on a single molecule using Kelvin probe force microscopy. It is hypothesized that KPFM can map the charge distribution to confirm the theoretical prediction of π-holes. The presence of a π-hole is expected to influence the adsorption of molecules on solid-state surfaces. Specifically, the π-hole should alter the electrostatic interaction between the molecule and a metallic surface. Consequently, the π-hole is predicted to change the adsorption height of the molecule on the substrate.

Methodological Details
The experiments were conducted at a temperature of 4.2 K using a commercial STM/nc-AFM microscope. Pt/Ir tips, sharpened by focused ion beam (FIB), were utilized and were further cleaned and shaped. The Au(111) substrate was prepared by repeated cycles of Ar+ sputtering (1 keV) and subsequent annealing at ~800 K. 9,10-Dichlorooctafluoroanthracene (FCl-An) and anthracene (An) molecules were sublimated with two Knudsen cells simultaneously. Scanning tunnelling microscopy (STM) images were acquired at a base temperature of 4.8 K. Noncontact atomic force microscopy (nc-AFM) was performed with a functionalized carbon monoxide (CO) tip. Kelvin Probe Force Microscopy (KPFM) records the spatial variation of the local contact potential difference (LCPD). LCPD maps were obtained by fitting a parabolic expression to frequency shift vs bias spectroscopies. The data was collected at constant height using the same CO functionalized tip for both molecules. Geometries were calculated using DFT-based methods implemented in the FHI-AIMS code. The PBE version of the GGA was employed for the exchange-correlation functional. Van der Waals correction based on the Tkatchenko-Scheffler method with Hirshfeld partitioning was applied. SAPT0 analysis was performed on a cluster model to provide the interaction energy decomposition scheme.

Procedures And Architectures
The qPlus sensor had a resonant frequency of approximately 30 kHz and a stiffness of approximately 1800 N/m. The oscillation amplitude was set to 200 pm for nc-AFM imaging. Both nc-AFM and KPFM images were captured in constant height mode. Each data point was acquired in approximately 3 seconds, with each parabola containing 600 points. The bias range for KPFM measurements was (-150, 400) mV. The acquisition height was chosen to be in the attractive regime to maximize the electrostatic contribution. Simulations used the Probe Particle (PP) model adapted to a CO-terminated tip. The lateral spring constant of the CO molecule was modelled as 0.25 N/m. The Au(111) slab consisted of 4 atomic layers. The surface supercell corresponded to the 6×6 unit cell of the unreconstructed Au(111) surface. For the supramolecular structure, a √39×√39 surface cell of Au(111) was constructed. Molecular orbitals were calculated for MP2/cc-pVTZ optimized geometries. SAPT0 calculations were made on the cluster models by the PSI4 program in cc-pVDZ basis set.

Key Results
The study experimentally confirms the existence of the π-hole in 9,10-Dichlorooctafluoroanthracene (FCl-An). The π-hole is absent in anthracene (An). The supramolecular assembly comprises a rhombic periodic structure with one An and two FCl-An molecules. The arrangement is dictated by attractive intermolecular electrostatic interactions between negatively charged fluorine atoms, sigmahole on chlorine, and positively charged hydrogen atoms. The simulated KPFM images match very well with the experimental evidence. The experimental images reproduce a characteristic bow-tie pattern in the central part of the FCl-An molecule. The difference between the minima of two Δf-z curves of An and FCl-An is 30 pm. The relative height of An above the Au(111) surface is 330 pm. The relative height of FCl-An above the Au(111) surface is 360 pm. The induced electron density is more significant in the interface between An molecule and metallic substrate. The induction energy describing stabilization energy due to electrostatic interaction is larger for An than for FCl-An.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The internal variation of the LCPD signal matches the distribution of the electrostatic potential calculated for a free-standing FCl-An molecule. This effect is associated with the heterogeneous charge distribution of the π-hole due to the different electronegativity of fluorine and chlorine. The presence of a π-hole increases the ionization potential of the molecule. The increased ionization potential inhibits the induction of the charge density at the molecule/metal interface. This results in weakened induced electrostatic interactions and, consequently, in larger adsorption height of the molecule. The study shows the potential of scanning microscopy for studying the internal charge distribution in molecules.
